title: The Shortest Loop in a Network
statement:
An undirected graph has `n` nodes numbered `0` to `n - 1` and the given `edges`; there is at most one edge between two nodes and no edge joins a node to itself. A **cycle** is a closed path that visits at least three different nodes and returns to its start without using any node twice.

Return the **length of the shortest cycle** (the number of edges, which equals the number of nodes on it), or `-1` if the graph has no cycle.
constraints: 0 <= len(edges) <= 5000, 0 <= a, b < n, a != b, no repeated edges

examples.explanation: The triangle 0 - 1 - 2 is a cycle of length 3; the path 2 - 3 - 4 hangs off it and is not part of any cycle.

hints.nudge: A breadth-first search from a node finds the shortest path to every other node. What does it mean when the search meets a node it has already seen, by an edge that is not the one it just came along?
hints.pattern: Breadth-first search from every node; whenever an edge leads to an already seen node that is not the parent, a cycle of length dist[u] + dist[v] + 1 passes through the start's search tree; keep the smallest over all starts.
hints.walkthrough: Listing every cycle is exponential. Use the fact that breadth-first search levels are shortest distances. During a search from s, when you look at an edge (u, v) and v has already been reached, and v is not the node u was reached from, then the two paths s -> u and s -> v together with the edge (u, v) contain a cycle of at most dist[u] + dist[v] + 1 edges. For the start that lies ON the shortest cycle this bound is exactly its length, and for every other start it is never smaller than the true shortest cycle, so taking the minimum over all starts gives the answer. The `parent` check avoids counting the edge you came along as a cycle (there are no repeated edges, so this is enough). Each search costs O(n + m), and there are n of them.
